Juvenile recruitment dynamics in the reef-dwelling Crown-of-thorns starfish Acanthaster planci are intimately tied to water temperature. Laboratory studies conducted at a stable ambient temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C] reveal that the bipinnaria larva typically completes its planktonic phase and undergoes settlement at an age of 38 days  under those thermal conditions. This relatively brief larval duration is characteristic of tropical echinoderms and stands in contrast to longer pelagic periods observed in temperate asteriid congeners. Following metamorphic climax, the recently metamorphosed juvenile starfish, derived from a fertilised ovum measuring roughly 0.15 millimeters in diameter, begins its benthic existence. The initial wet weight of these post-metamorphic individuals at the moment of birth into the juvenile stage is exceedingly modest, calculated from egg volume to be approximately 0.0000017 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000017 grams], reflecting the tiny size of the yolk-dependent embryo from which they develop.

Growth during the initial benthic phase is substantial, with sub-adult individuals progressing steadily toward their characteristic large body size. Field surveys of mature populations indicate that the maximum body diameter attained by this species, its ultimate diameter, reaches 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters], placing Acanthaster planci among the largest known asteroid species globally. This remarkable size is facilitated by a diet almost exclusively composed of scleractinian coral tissue, which provides a nutrient-rich resource base. The progression from a minute post-metamorphic juvenile weighing less than two millionths of a gram to a massive coral predator spanning nearly three-quarters of a meter involves a multi-year period of accelerated somatic growth. Such a dramatic increase in body dimensions over the life cycle underscores the extraordinary scope for ontogenetic niche shifts that characterise this keystone predator on Indo-Pacific reef systems.

Reproductive development in Acanthaster planci follows a trajectory tied to both body size and thermal regime. Individuals at 29 °C [T = 29 °C] only initiate gonadal maturation after a substantial juvenile growth period: the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth] under these warm-water conditions. This extended pre-pubertal interval is interpreted as an adaptive strategy allowing the starfish to amass sufficient body mass to support the high energetic demands of gametogenesis. The diameter at puberty, that is, the central disc size at which gonadal activity commences, has been measured at approximately 19 centimeters [Lp = approximately 19 centimeters] in wild populations from the Great Barrier Reef. This size threshold for reproductive readiness is not unusual among large echinoderms, though it is reached relatively early compared to the maximum body diameter the species can achieve over its lifetime.

A full accounting of the species' life-history requires characterising its eventual reproductive output and the physiological condition of breeding adults. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), which expresses gonad mass as a proportion of total body mass, was recorded at 22% [GSI = 22%] in spawning-capable individuals maintained at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. Such a high index is consistent with the species' strategy of broadcast fertilisation, where enormous numbers of gametes are released into the water column during synchronized spawning events. These aggregative spawning episodes involve dense concentrations of adults and can result in the release of millions of ova per female per event.

Longevity data for this large asteroid suggest a surprisingly rapid life cycle relative to its ultimate diameter. The lifespan of Acanthaster planci under natural reef conditions at 29 °C [T = 29 °C] has been estimated at approximately 6205 days [am = approximately 6205 days], a duration equivalent to roughly 17 years, though most individuals in outbreak populations may experience higher mortality due to disease or predation before reaching this maximum age. This lifespan, while considerable for an invertebrate, is shorter than that reported for many other large-bodied echinoderms of comparable ultimate diameter. The combination of a relatively brief pre-reproductive delay, high gonado somatic index during adulthood, and moderate longevity suggests a life-history strategy prioritising early and intense reproductive output over extended somatic persistence. Such demographic parameters help explain the species' well-documented capacity for population irruptions following larval recruitment events.
